newsitem.title: UK: UK's Blair-what are his priorities in government?.
newsitem.headline: UK's Blair-what are his priorities in government?.

text.p: Labour leader Tony Blair, planning for power after 18 years in opposition, has scrupulously avoided making grandiose pledges that he might not be able to keep.
To some of Blair's supporters, the five basic commitments he has made on health, education, juvenile crime, youth unemployment and economic policy smack of minimalism.

Left wingers also worry that economics spokesman Gordon Brown's solemn promise to freeze income tax and stick to the Conservatives' tough public spending targets will tie Labour's hands if it wins the election, now just weeks away.

But Labour officials insist that playing down expectations should not be read as a lack of ambition and say they are preparing a sheaf of policies for the first year of a Labour government that would mark a decisive break with the past.
Following is a summary, drawn from published Labour documents and conversations with party officials, of the main early initiatives to be expected from a Blair government.
EDUCATION -- Blair, convinced Britain has fallen dangerously behind its partners, has said an education bill would be the flagship of his first legislative programme.
He plans to divert resources to education and put the education ministry on a par with the other three great departments of state -- treasury, home affairs and the Foreign Office.

"The passion of a government I lead will be education. This is because a just society and a strong economy depend on the excellence of the education we provide to all our children," he said on February 3.

The bill will seek to reduce class sizes for five-seven year olds to 30 or under by using money saved from phasing out a scheme that helps low-income families to send their children to private schools.

The voucher scheme for nursery school places would be scrapped. Labour also wants to establish summer literacy camps, national homework guidelines and individual learning accounts to help adults gain skills.

CONSTITUTIONAL CHANGE -- Labour's business managers want to pass a paving bill before the summer recess to set the stage for referenda on a parliament for Scotland with tax-raising powers and an assembly for Wales with more modest powers.
Blair says: "We are planning the most extensive package of constitutional change ever proposed by a British government."
Devolution will take priority over plans to end the voting rights of hereditary peers in the House of Lords and over possible consideration of changes to Britain's voting system.

WINDFALL TAX -- With Brown tied to the Conservatives' income tax rates and spending plans, the centrepiece of the interim budget Labour plans to unveil within weeks of the election is its windfall tax on the excess profits of privatised utilities.

Labour, wary of legal challenges, has not specified which firms will be subject to the one-off tax, which could raise 5-10 billion pounds. The party says it will first consult, once in power, with utility regulators and interested parties.
"In principle all privatised utilties will be considered as candidates for the levy without fear or favour," Labour's deputy leader, John Prescott, has said.
EMPLOYMENT -- The proceeds of the windfall tax are earmarked for a scheme to get 250,000 under-25s who have been unemployed for more than six months off welfare and into work or training.
It will also finance a tax rebate of 75 pounds a week to employers who take on people who have been out of work for more than two years.
A planned Fair Employment Act would fulfil Labour's pledge to set up a low-pay commission grouping employers, unions and independent experts to fix a rate for a national minimum wage.

Although Blair has promised not to turn the clock back on the bulk of the Conservatives' industrial relations reforms, the Act would strengthen some trade union rights as well as equal opportunities and health and safety legislation.
Employers, for instance, would be required to recognise a union if more than half the workforce voted for recognition.
In a symbolic move, staff at the government's GCHQ spy centre in Cheltenham would be permitted to join a trade union.
WELFARE -- Blair wants to make an early start on reform of Britain's 90 billion pound social security budget, with the aim of getting people off welfare and into work.

"There will be no option of a life permanently on full benefit. Where there is a suitable offer, people will be expected to take this up. That is fair. Rights and responsibilities go together," Blair said in a keynote speech in Amsterdam in January.
An early priority could be Britain's one million unemployed lone parents, for whom Blair's plans include job counselling and better child-care provision.

HEALTH -- Labour plans to make a start on restructuring the internal market in the National Health Service introduced by the Conservatives, which it says has turned doctors into accountants and helped to create a two-tier NHS.

Measures such as replacing GP fund-holding with a system called GP commissioning aim to promote cooperation rather than competition so resources can be shifted from administration to front-line patient care, reducing hospital waiting lists.

A minister for public health will be appointed, tobacco advertising banned and a new set of Health of the Nation targets drawn up, to reflect impact of poverty and inequality on health, to coincide with the 50th birthday of the NHS in 1998.

FINANCIAL SERVICES -- Labour's Treasury team is hoping to find parliamentary time for a building societies bill and a bill to streamline regulation by folding all the City of London's self-regulatory organisations into a super-Securities and Investments Board.
HOME AFFAIRS - Fast-track punishment for persistent young offenders is one of Labour's five early pledges. It wants to halve the time from arrest to sentencing.
Other early priorities will be a clampdown on noisy and disruptive neighbours and legislation requiring the police and local authorities to implement crime prevention projects.
DEFENCE - Labour has promised to conduct a full-scale review of Britain's defence needs but denies Conservative claims that this will be a smoke-screen for further cuts in arms spending.

"The review we propose will be foreign policy-led, first assessing our likely overseas commitments and interests and then establishing how our forces should be deployed to meet them," Blair wrote in the Daily Telegraph in February. "My pledge to our Armed Forces is that we will offer a period of stability."
EUROPE/FOREIGN POLICY -- Labour has virtually ruled out joining the single currency in 1999 but acknowledges it would be hard to stay out for long if monetary union succeeded.

While keeping its EMU options open, foreign affairs spokesman Robin Cook is determined to mend fences with Europe after years of Conservative hostility that he says has pandered to prejudice and betrayed Britain's national interest.
"Britain will get more out of the European Union through cooperation than from confrontation," Cook said on February 5.

Labour is confident of reaching an agreement at the Amsterdam Inter-Governmental Conference in June, which will wrap up negotiations on how to streamline the EU's institutions, and will further demonstrate its Euro-credentials by signing the bloc's social chapter on common workplace standards.
Cook has said his priority as foreign secretary would be to use Britain's diplomatic muscle to boost trade. To that end, he has promised to name businessmen to key ambassadorial posts.

Within a year of being elected, a Labour government would have an unparalleled opportunity to make a diplomatic mark, for Britain will chair summits of the Commonwealth, the Group of Seven and EU-Asian leaders. It will also have a six-month stint as EU president just as EMU preparations reach a climax.
MISCELLANEOUS - With extra spending ruled out, the hunt is on for measures that would not cost anything but would demonstrate to voters that Labour can make a difference.
To root out sleaze in politics, for example, Labour has promised to ban secret funding from overseas and to require the disclosure of the source of donations over 10,000 pounds.
It will also give the head of the National Audit Office wider powers to hunt down wasted taxpayers' money.
Proceeds from the National Lottery, which Labour calls the "people's money", would be distributed more equitably with a possible cap on jackpots.
London, whose council was scrapped by Margaret Thatcher, has been promised a strategic planning authority and an elected mayor.
